utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll resume now after the weekend break. I would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, of the Defence, the accused, and everyone else present in the courtroom. We have a witness scheduled for today, but before the witness is brought into the courtroom, I will now render my oral decision about the documents. We have provided the interpreters with a copy -- no, in fact we haven't. I will read it out slowly, because it is quite long, and I would like to ask both parties to take good note of what has been decided. I would like to remind you that the Prosecution has requested that exhibits in its consolidated list be admitted into evidence. Defence counsel has contested a significant number of these exhibits. They are opposed to them being tendered into evidence because they claim that they lack relevance and are not reliable. The explanations provided included a list of documents and categories in which they explained the reasons for which they were not satisfied with these documents. The Trial Chamber has decided that the originals will be provided to the Chamber and a chronological list of the documents will be established. The Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution complied with this request. Before taking a final decision with regard to the request made by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber has decided on the following measures. These measures will be divided into three broad categories. Category A: The Trial Chamber, given the agreement reached between the parties, requests that the Prosecution provide all information on the documents provided to it by governments, either of their own accord or in response to a request submitted by them. That is the first measure that we have decided on. The second one is as follows: The Trial Chamber requests that the Prosecution should call as witnesses archivists who are responsible for the Sarajevo and Zenica archives. We request that the Prosecution, to the extent that this is possible, inform the Trial Chamber of any material it has in its possession that proves that these documents were sent and received. Fourthly, we request that the Prosecution calls as a witness a former high-ranking member of the military from the BH army who held the position of commander in order to testify with regard to the drafting of orders, the transmission of orders, the power of delegating, and to testify with regard to the orders followed in 1993. Fifthly, we request that the Prosecution provide the Trial Chamber with examples of the accused's signatures. Sixthly, we request that the Prosecution inform the Trial Chamber in writing on the origin of the documents provided by the governments, with the exception of the archives from Sarajevo and Zagreb. And finally, we request that the Prosecution provide all the operational logs and all the war diaries with full translations into English and into French. So that is as far as A is concerned. Under B, the Trial Chamber has also decided that the Prosecution will provide next Friday a list of witnesses in a position to authenticate the documents and the Prosecution shall make reference to the documents that regard these witnesses. Under 2, the Prosecution is requested to provide the documents missing from the binders, including the missing translations. And to this effect the Trial Chamber will provide via the Chamber's legal officer a list of the missing documents or the documents that are not complete. The Prosecution will also confer -- will also consult in order to respond to this request the list established by the Defence on the 19th of April, 2004. Thirdly, the Prosecution, after having carried out a strict examination of the documents provided, should provide the documents that are currently missing, the documents which have only been partially disclosed, and in particular the documents referred to in the annex. Fourthly, as far as the videotapes are concerned, the videotapes will be broadcast in public at a subsequent hearing. The Prosecution shall provide, if it has not yet done so, a full transcript of the text on these tapes. When the tapes are broadcast, the Trial Chamber will give both parties the floor. If following a debate between both parties there's any serious doubt as to the authenticity of the videotapes, the Trial Chamber shall reserve the right to request that the Prosecution call the person who made the video as a witness, given that Mr. Angus Hay and Jason Medley, two witnesses, have been scheduled, the tapes that concern them will be broadcast on the day that they are heard as witnesses. The video on the Mujahedin may, if the Prosecution deems that this is useful, be broadcast when witness Hogg is heard. And under number 5, concerning the telephone intercepts. The Prosecution will disclose the origin and the manner in which these intercepts were forwarded. They will provide us with information on this. The Defence will then state what its position is with regard to these intercepts. Under C - and this is the third part of the decision - the Trial Chamber has decided that the witness Mika Tauru should testify about how the sketches presented by a witness who has already been heard were made. The Trial Chamber hereby informs both parties that it has decided, in a written decision which will soon be provided to the Prosecution and to the Defence, that the witness (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: And finally, the Trial Chamber requests that with regard to the eight binders of noncontested documents, of documents that haven't been contested by the Defence - these documents have also been admitted by the Trial Chamber - we request that the Prosecution provide the missing documents. And with regard to this matter, the Trial Chamber would like to request that the Prosecution provide as soon as possible document P332/E -- for document P332/E the annexes mentioned in the document dated the 1st of February, 1993, under number ERN 03086589. So I would like to ask both parties to carefully reread the transcript because there are a number of measures that we have decided on, and following these measures, once these measures have been accomplished, the Trial Chamber will render a final decision concerning the documents. And following this decision, it seems that the -- it is evident Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the videos will be broadcast in public, and there are three witnesses who can provide support for presenting these videos. And in any event, the videos will be broadcast, and after they have been broadcast, the Prosecution and the Defence will take the floor to express their position on the videos. So the same is the case for the telephone intercepts. And on the basis of the transcripts which were noted, the Prosecution will inform the Trial Chamber of how these transcripts were made and forwarded, and the Defence will express its position. The Trial Chamber has decided that a number of witnesses should be called in order to testify about the documents, as I have already said. So the Trial Chamber, having examined all the binders, realised that there were certain missing documents. Either there were documents that weren't translated or there were annexes that were missing or the documents themselves were incomplete, which is why we have mentioned in our decision that we are requesting the totality of the documents, complete documents. Please read the transcript through carefully, and naturally it is the Prosecution's duty to have the witnesses come and to fit them into the schedule that they have planned. But we have requested that a measure be taken by next Friday in this particular case. In 24 hours or 48 hours, we will render our written decision about the witness who will be called. We said that the archivists had to appear before the Court in order to authenticate the documents that are being provided, and in addition with regard to the war diaries or the -- and the logbooks, it is necessary to have all of them. And we must also have full translations of these documents. And to make sure that there are no uncertainties, we are requesting that we have translations from B/C/S into English and a translation of B/C/S into French, in order to be able to compare the English and French translation. We don't want to have any doubts as to the contents of these diaries or logbooks. So this is our decision, and the final decision about the documents will be taken later. Without wasting any more time, we have a witness. Could the usher call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I would first like to check that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If that is the case, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were called here as a witness for the Prosecution. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would like you to tell me your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bryan Watters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me your date of birth, your place of birth, and your nationality, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of October, 1953, in Tiko, British Cameroon, and I'm British.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are British.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me what your current position is, what your current profession is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a serving military officer in the British Army. I'm a colonel. And I'm currently deputy director of the British Defence Leadership Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What position did you hold in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the second-in-command of the British Battalion, 1 Cheshire Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified with regard to the events of 1993, either before an international or a national court, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've testified here before, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember which case you testified and were you called as a witness for the Prosecution or for the Defence or as a witness for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a Prosecution witness in three previous trials, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me the names of these cases, if you can remember them

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Blaskic case, sir; the case of Kordic; and the case concerning the massacre at Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you will be testifying now, could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have testified on a number of occasions, you are perfectly familiar with the procedure followed before this Tribunal. Nevertheless, I would like to remind you that as you are being called here as a witness for the Prosecution, you will first of all have to answer questions put to you by members of the Prosecution, who are to your right. You have certainly met members of the Prosecution before today, in order to prepare for your testimony. After this phase has been concluded, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will conduct their cross-examination. And you will immediately realise that the questions put to you by the Defence are not of the same kind as those put to you by members of the Prosecution. The purpose of the questions put to you by Defence counsel is to check the credibility of what you say or to obtain any useful information for the Defence. After this stage has been concluded, the Prosecution may re-examine you. The three Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions if they think that this might be useful. As a rule, the Judges prefer to wait for the end of the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination, and re-examination before asking you their questions. When a Judge asks you some questions, the Prosecution and the Defence may also ask you questions based on the answers that you provide to the Judges' questions. As you are used to this procedure, you know that the procedure is mainly oral, and this is why the answers that you provide are so important. To the extent that this is possible, try to be clear, precise, and concise when answering questions. If a question seems to be too complicated or incomprehensible, ask the person putting the questions to you to rephrase it. If the question seems to be too complex to you, take your time before you respond. If you feel that there are difficulties of any kind, you can inform the Trial Chamber of the fact. I would also like to remind you of two other important factors: First of all, given that a witness has made a solemn declaration, he should not give false testimony. If false testimony is given, a witness could be prosecuted, because false testimony is a violation which is subject to penalties. And secondly - but this should not really concern you; nevertheless, I want to point it out - when a witness answers a question, the witness may refuse to answer a question if by answering it the witness provides information that could be incriminating. In such a case, the witness can refuse to answer the question. This is common-law procedure. But it is possible for the Trial Chamber to compel the witness to answer the question. Nevertheless, the witness is guaranteed a form of immunity if he answers the question. So roughly speaking, this is the procedure that will be followed in the course of your testimony. We will have the entire day for your testimony, and I will now give the floor to Mr. Withopf, who will be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conducting the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber briefly summarise your military career within the British Army, with a focus on your deployments abroad, if any.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Sir, I've been a professional military officer for 32 years. I first deployed on operations in 1974 to Northern Ireland, where I subsequently served five and a half years on operations in different capacities. I served in the former Rhodesia as part of the British Commonwealth Monitoring Force, deploying there to bring the war to an end. I served for a year in Central America, in Belize, supporting the Belizean government in maintaining their national integrity and supporting operations against narcotics. I served a year in Hong Kong in support of the Hong Kong government in illegal immigration operations on the border with China. I served in Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the United Nations in 1993. I subsequently served in Kenya, and for two years I served in Brunei, Dar El-Salaam as the commander of our jungle warfare school. And that probably does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. In respect to Brunei, did you experience anything that was connected to the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I was serving in Brunei immediately prior to deploying to Bosnia. Other than reading about it in the paper with specific interest as obviously my own regiment was there and rather startled to see a picture of an old friend of my future commanding officer in the newspapers, Brunei Dar El-Salaam is a Muslim country and there was a considerable feeling of moral support for the Muslim peoples within Bosnia-Herzegovina and there were regular recollections of money at road junctions. And on occasion, I was stopped at a road junction and asked to contribute to the Muslim cause in Bosnia, which I found slightly ironic, as I was shortly to deploy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the commanding positions you held over the years at the various levels.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm an infantry soldier. I began my infantry career commanding a platoon, which is 30 soldiers; I then became a specialist platoon commander in what we call an anti-tank platoon. We had a variety of weapons designed to destroy tanks, and I commanded those. I was a company second-in-command of an armoured -- of a light infantry and mechanised infantry. I was a company commander of a light infantry company. I was a second-in-command of the battalion, including our period in Bosnia-Herzegovina and later in Northern Ireland. I commanded the battalion as the commanding officer for two years in Northern Ireland, a period in the United Kingdom, and a period in Kenya. And today, although a full colonel, I don't have a command position. I'm working in a education establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You mentioned it earlier on, sir, but can you repeat it for the sake of the transcript. What was your rank whilst deployed in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I was a major, and my appointment was that of the senior major within the group, second-in-command to the battalion commander, and also the de facto Chief of Staff of the battalion group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what's your rank today, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please provide the Trial Chamber with some information in respect to your current responsibilities, being the deputy director of Defence Leadership Centre in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm specifically responsible -- the centre itself is charged by the Ministry of Defence with improving leadership throughout the Ministry of Defence and the Army, Navy, Air Force and the civil service, and I'm specifically the director of our defence strategic-leadership program for newly-promoted brigadiers, commodores, air commodores, and senior civil servants, those entering the first level of strategic leadership within our defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Colonel, let's move on to your deployment with UNPROFOR BritBat in Central Bosnia. Can you please inform us from when to when you were deployed with UNPROFOR BritBat.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I arrived in Bosnia at the beginning of February 1993. My battalion had already been there for a couple of months, and I replaced the existing second-in-command on a already preplanned rotation. And I left halfway through May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, I understand you were the second-in-command?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. What that means is I'm the deputy commander and command the organisation if the commanding officer isn't present, as well as coordinating the staff efforts of our intelligence - although on that tour that function was described as military information - operations, and logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber, Colonel, who was the commanding officer at the time you were deployed in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: He was then Lieutenant Colonel Robert Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To what extent, Colonel, were you already familiar with the situation in Central Bosnia at the time you arrived; and did you have a chance to familiarise yourself with the military situation after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Prior to arrival, I'd found scant information, other than what I'd read in the newspapers, although I did find a book by somebody called Misha Glennie, which I read. As part of my professional responsibilities, I'd also studied the Partizan operations in Yugoslavia during the Second World War. And so I had an understanding of some of the fundamental principles of the terrain, et cetera. On arrival, my predecessor, Major Tim Park, and I undertook a reconnaissance of our deployed areas, and I also in speaking to the various military commanders that we encountered, I also attended the first of the Busovaca commission meetings, run by the ECMM, on the 13th of February, which I found very useful, because I there had the opportunity to speak to the senior commanders within our area of responsibility from the BiH and the HVO. And then I also tapped into the considerable source of information that our military-information cell had been able to gather and also discussed with our company commanders and Italian liaison officers, to familiarise myself with personalities, military objectives of the different warring factions, the geography, and history of that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, in order to summarise what you just said, that within a few weeks after your arrival you were familiar with the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I'd say I was familiar with the situation on the ground. My understanding of the complexities of the situation evolved during my entire time there. I was still learning when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform us, Colonel, where were you based? Where were you headquartered at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: In Vitez, in the Lasva Valley, which is where the battalion headquarters was based. Our companies were based in different parts of our areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where exactly were the companies based?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: One company to the north in Tuzla; another company in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the area of responsibility of BritBat.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: It was a large area. Depending on the conditions, it could take us anything up to 12 to 15 hours, for example, to get from Tuzla to Vitez or vice versa. And Gornji Vakuf would take probably a morning or an afternoon. None of the arterial roads were usable, because most of them were in range of Serb artillery. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Sorry. And the area was essentially bounded by front lines, between the Serbs, if you like, on the outside of our area, and the ABiH or the HVO or an alliance of the two on the inside of our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of BritBat you just described, was there an overlap with the area of responsibility of the ABiH 3rd Corps? And if so, to what extent?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. The 3rd Corps was based in Zenica, which was within our area of responsibility. And the majority of our interaction with the ABiH was through the 3rd Corps, either through brigade commanders or the corps commander himself or his deputy. And we also liaised with -- I think it was 4th Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please briefly inform us about the structure of BritBat and the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: BritBat was based on a British armoured infantry battalion equipped with just over 50 Warrior fighting vehicles. We had specialist anti-armour and mortar platoons. We had been brought up from what we would describe as a peacetime establishment in our base in Fallingbostle in Germany to war establishment, with the inclusion of an additional 100 or so soldiers from the 2nd Battalion of the Royal Irish Regiment, and they reinforced our existing 54 Warriors. In addition, we had a Royal Engineer Squadron, a squadron from the 9th-12th Lancers, which was a light-reconnaissance regiment equipped with the Scimitar light tank. We also had the specialist signals detachment to enable our reeled communication to the UK, and we also had a -- what we called the mobile surgical team. That was a fully equipped surgical team with a full range of surgeons and other medics. We also had other additional small organisations to help with our logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform us about the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: The chain of command. Within the 1 Cheshire Group?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: The chain of command was the commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Stewart, who commanded directly each of the company commanders, Headquarters Company, Alpha Company, Bravo Company, Charlie Company, support company elements, the Royal Engineers and the 9th-12th Lancers. And he would command those directly. And if he was present and commanding, I would act as his Chief of Staff. If he was not present, then as his deputy I would assume command and command in his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And was there a chain of command within UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. We were commanded from Headquarters UNPROFOR in Kiseljak, command by General Philippe Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please, Colonel, inform the Trial Chamber about the mission and the goals of BritBat or the tasks and the purpose why BritBat was operating in the area.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's an interesting question. When we were deployed, the whole of UNPROFOR was deploying at the same time, so there wasn't an infrastructure into which we plugged which had established missions and tasks and purposes. And so we were operating, if you will, within a sort of overarching understanding of the intent of UNPROFOR, which was to do its best for the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to support the other United Nations agencies that were there. And so if you will, that was our understanding of the reason we were there. We ourselves refined that and gave ourselves the mission essentially of facilitating the distribution of humanitarian aid in order to save life. And that conformed with our doctrine of mission command, where we set ourselves and our subordinate organisation missions consisting of a task and a purpose working with an overall superior's command and intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What at the time, Colonel, what were the essentials and the keys to ensure the success of your task and its purpose?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: The commanding officer articulated that in what we describe as a scheme of manoeuvre, and that was to create across our area of responsibility an overlay of security on the key routes that would enable the UNHCR to distribute humanitarian aid wherever they felt it was required. And we would use our combat power to interdict any area of fighting that would threaten other members of the United Nations and prevent them facilitating the distribution of humanitarian aid. We tended to prefer not to escort single convoys by putting vehicles at the front and end of them, although on occasion we did do that, in areas of specifically high turbulence or threat. We preferred to patrol widely and purposefully to deter violence against the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just mentioning, Colonel, that you were creating an overlap of security. Was the gathering of information a means to create such an overlap of security?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. Within the scheme of manoeuvre, as well as a means of creating this overlay of security, a web of security, if you will, critical to that concept was the deployment of a number of liaison officers whose task was to get to know political and military commanders in their specific area of responsibility in order to learn as much as possible about their agendas and their areas, to facilitate the commanding officer or myself in future discussions; and also, again, to build trust on the impartiality of BritBat and UNPROFOR and our commitment to trying to bring peace to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just talking about the liaison officers, sir. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber how and where they were deployed and were they also deployed within 3rd Corps units -- ABiH 3rd Corps units?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: We had specific areas that individual liaison officers were responsible for: The Lasva Valley area, the Tuzla area, the Kakanj sort of area; Vitez, specifically within the Lasva Valley; and sometimes an individual whose area became very active would be reinforced with another person to help him. So for example, when Vitez and Travnik became very active, we would try and support that particular liaison officer in his task in those two towns. And also in the sort of Zenica area as well. The specific liaison with the 3rd Corps headquarters, although there was a liaison officer who focussed on Zenica and initially created the introductions, those liaisons with the senior members of the HVO or the ABiH were routinely the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Which would have been Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Robert Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. You were just mentioning the Lasva Valley area. How in geographical terms would you describe the Lasva Valley area?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: From Turbe through Travnik down through Vitez down to Busovaca, generally. And Busovaca we'd call the beginning of the Kiseljak valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would you include Zenica in this area or --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah. Sorry, I went over Zenica. It's between sort of Busovaca and Travnik. Indeed. Zenica, if you like, from our perspective was the centre of the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Earlier on, Colonel, you were briefly touching on the issue in respect to the difference between information and intelligence. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what actually the difference is about.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: It's a slightly semantic difference on one level. Our organisation has an intelligence cell headed up by a captain and that was reinforced with other specialist intelligence personnel. In our role in UNPROFOR, the United Nations doesn't run intelligence, it runs information. And so our intelligence cell was converted to a military information cell. And although it was a subtle difference, it was an important difference because we were not gathering information and processing it into intelligence about our enemies. We were gathering information widely -- and as very much part of our scheme of manoeuvre was the gathering of information -- and this information would then build up pictures to enable us to understand things day by day, week by week; and these were concentrated, articulated within the military information summary that we would issue each day, which was an assessment of our understanding on that particular day. And we would also pass this information up our chain of command and down our chain of command to spread our understanding and coordination of information. Central to our scheme of manoeuvre was this understanding of the situation going through information. Every patrol, every commander, every logistician who was deployed as part of UNPROFOR would be debriefed on our return as to what they had seen, what they believed they had seen, asked to try and articulate what it is they interpreted by what they had seen, and all this information was gathered and cross-referenced to try and create a broad picture of understanding within our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, may I please ask you a number of follow-up questions. Would it be fair to say whatever is called "information" in a milinfosum is in fact intelligence in military terms?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's why I said the difference is slightly semantic. We have a very formal process of turning information into intelligence, called an intelligence cycle. I'm not a specific expert in that. I'm not an intelligence officer. You could describe it as intelligence. We maintained our view throughout our time in Bosnia that that was military information, and we didn't classify it, which we would do with intelligence. We didn't -- we passed it in its raw form with comment up and down our chain of command. We didn't ascribe to it the rigour of the procedures for judging information as intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Although not being an intelligence officer, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what was your part, if any, in respect to the gathering and disseminating of information.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: As all other members of BritBat, I had a responsibility when I was patrolling or visiting to record what I'd seen and heard and report that back, as any other member of the group. As the Chief of Staff, I was responsible for the coordination of the intelligence cell with -- sorry, the information -- military information cell with operations to ensure that the information we had was available too. And also they would act as a commentator on the value of some of the information we have and sometimes would advise on the -- from an operational point of view, on the utility of some of the information we had and how it met the operational sense of what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Colonel, you were already touching on the issue that BritBat at the time made efforts to ensure the reliability of the information gathered. Were double-checked made or cross-checks made? And can you please explain to the Trial Chamber if so what sort of checks were made.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: It was cross-referencing different sources of information, and I can give you an example. A number of reports came in about a particularly -- an area we were quite sensitive about, which was a particular road junction, and our understanding that there was a HVO sort of prisoner-of-war centre, and we used to keep an eye on that. And a number of reports came. For example, one report from a patrol said they'd seen some men digging in a field with a grid reference; another report came in saying that a patrol had seen some HVO soldiers guarding a group of prisoners walking down the road in whatever direction, and the prisoners were carrying shovels. And another -- several other reports similar to those. And we were able to draw the deductions that the HVO were using BiH prisoners to dig trenches, military defensive positions, in a particular area. And that, again, caused several comments. One was the fact that this was an illegal act against the Geneva Convention, and we reported that to the UNHCR and to the ICRC. It was a combat indicator to us that the HVO, by digging defensive positions, were expecting some form of military activity in that area. And that is a sort of small example of how a number of different reports could begin to contribute to the picture, where any one on their own would not be necessarily significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And after having made such cross-checks and cross-references, were you satisfied -- or did the information gathered, did it serve the purpose to enable BritBat to achieve its mission purpose?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: It was an important part of our understanding of the situation and the understanding of the situation was central to our conducting of our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber how your average work day looked like, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I did have a few of what you could call average work days. There weren't many. We worked on average about an 18- to 20-hour day and would take four hours or so sleep, maybe five or six, depending, in every 24 hours. And we ran shift systems within our key areas, the operations centre, the milinfo centre, and so on. And as the second-in-command, I would choose to sleep at whatever point in the 24 hours I felt was the quietest time. I would try and do that in the dark, if I could. So it's very difficult to give you a -- you know, it wasn't 9.00 till 5.00, sort of thing. I was there seven days a week from the day I arrived until the day I left immersed in what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was 1800 hours a particular point in time during a day?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: In terms of routine, we would try and establish certain routines, like mealtimes, and 1800 hours was a time-out, if you like, where the commanding officer or myself, if he wasn't there - and he would endeavour to be there - would sit down with the liaison officers, who were tasked to endeavour to be there, and there had to be a very good reason why they weren't, and with the available company commanders, milinfo staff and operations staff and have a coordinating conference where each of the liaison officers would report on what they had seen and heard during the day, as would the operations staff, the milinfo staff. And it enabled the commanding officer to get a verbal brief and be able to cross-question people as to the situation in the preceding 24 hours. So it would be 1800 hours to 1800 hours. And it was an important part and, if you like, of what we would describe as sort of the battle rhythm of our organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Did this meeting, did it provide the participants of the meeting with a comprehensive picture -- did the meeting, sir, did it provide the participants of the meeting with a comprehensive picture of the events that had happened during a particular day on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did, Colonel, did this information, this comprehensive information which was provided during the 1800-hours meetings, did it finally form part of the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Although, it wasn't the milinfosum wasn't the product of this meeting. The milinfosum was normally produced to reflect sort of other activities as well. But it certainly was a capturing of our understanding for the preceding 24 hours in Gornji Vakuf, Tuzla and Vitez. The information from Tuzla and Gornji Vakuf would come by radio and would be presented either by the milinfo staff or the operations staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, Colonel, who was actually supposed to read the milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: All commanders, and we sent them also up our chain of command to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already touched on this issue earlier on briefly. In respect to the milinfosums, were facts, non-corroborated information, analysis and comments, were they distinguished?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: We would try to distinguish them just for our own benefit. And remember, the milinfosum was essentially for our own benefit and also for the benefit of our chain of command, to inform them from a milinfosum/intelligence perspective as to what we thought, as to posed to the daily situation report, which was totally factual. And the summation of the day would be gleaned from reading both of the reports. And the difference between the milinfosum and the situation report is the milinfosum would contain comment and hypothesis, while the situation report tended to deal just in facts. And also the milinfosum when published was a reflection of our understanding; but quite often two or three days, you know, what we thought earlier in the milinfosum, we had received additional information that would quite often cause us to re-examine and realise that what we'd thought, for example, on one day may not be an actual reflection of what happened and we hadn't gathered a more informed view for a number of days. So if you like, it was our sort of best bet on that day as to what our milinfosum team thought was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And in the event there was a re-examination, was the re-examination then reflected in one of the next milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: If there was a point in doing it. If the whole thing was overtaken by events, then we just let it go and focussed on the current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Let's move on to a different subject, namely the military situation within the area of responsibility of the ABiH 3rd Corps. Did I understand you correctly, Colonel, that the area of responsibility of BritBat was overlapping to a certain, if not a high extent, with the area of responsibility of the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber which army at the time of your arrival in Vitez in early February 1993, which army could be described as being the more dominant army?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: The Serb army, the Bosnian Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And talking about the ABiH and the HVO, which one was the more dominant in early 1993 or in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I think that's quite a difficult question, because I -- you'd have to define what you mean by "dominant."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Which one was on the attacking side, on the attacking move?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: In February 1993, when I arrived, the BiH and HVO were essentially on the defence. Following a series of Serb advances - notably, the fall of Jajce springs to mind just before I'd arrived, and we were dealing in February with a large number of sort of refugees from Jajce and Banja Luka, that the Serbs were sort of transporting to and then abandoning in the front lines behind Turbe; and a similar situation manifested itself later over towards Tuzla, with the Serb fighting in the area of Srebrenica. The BiH and the HVO were conducting counterattacks along the front lines, and I've never really reflected on which I thought was doing the most of that. At a guess, I would probably say it was the BiH who had a predominance of sort of infantry, whereas the HVO had a pre-dominance of sort of artillery and armour, and "artillery" I use in a very broad sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At what point in time, sir, in your view, did the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH break out?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: From my personal perspective, things began to go -- there were -- the alliance between the two held strongest where the imminent Serb threat was greatest. Where the Serb threat wasn't great, there was less of a unity of purpose between the two military groups -- military forces. From about the 1st of April, 1993, which was the declaration of the NATO no-fly zone, we had a series of incidents involving ourselves and the Serbs. We came under artillery fire from them and we also, at the behest, personal behest of General Morillon, sent a reconnaissance force to a place called Konjevic Polje, which ended up losing some of its armoured vehicles. And I went to Zvornik to recover the vehicles. And while I was in Zvornik things were taking place in Travnik, notably the visit of Mate Boban. And following that, there were a series of murders of BiH soldiers by HVO predominantly, although there were also some HVO soldiers murdered by BiH soldiers, we understood. And that -- and then there was a general -- in the view of the liaison officer for sort of Travnik and Vitez and Turbe, there was a general worsening of the relationship. And this was also -- had to be viewed, which was one of the things that we made attempts to do -- this also had to be viewed within the bigger picture of the, you know, what was going on beyond the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina, most notably various proposals that were on the world stage for potential solutions to the war in Bosnia, and notably the Vance Owen peace initiative, which itself appeared to be contributing to the increased tension between the Muslim people and the Croat people, the BiH and the HVO. And there were a series of situations leading up to -- I think it was the 16th of April, when we heard reports from our logistics organisation, which was closer than we were to Vitez, of mortar -- considerable mortar fire and small arms fire from Vitez and its environs up towards Kruscica, and it was at that point that we realised that something had gone very wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that in your view the ABiH-HVO conflict started at around the first half of April 1993. Would this summarise --

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: -- what you just said?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And making reference to what you said earlier on, would it be fair to say that the HVO was the stronger army in terms of military equipment and the ABiH was the stronger army in respect to the manpower?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I would take that -- I agree with that as a generalisation, not specifically in the Vitez and its environs in the Lasva Valley at that point in April, because, for example, 3rd Corps was heavily engaged in fighting the Serbs in the east or consolidating their position in the light of some Serb advances. And so there was an imbalance in Central Bosnia at that time where the HVO had a -- outnumbered, both in terms of personnel and materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time later on during your tour in Central Bosnia when the situation changed? And if so, as to when and how did it change?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Sorry, do you mean broadly the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The situation within the area of responsibility of the ABiH 3rd Corps. And in particular, in the area you were just describing.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Do you mean the -- sort of the situation where the HVO launched what we certainly believed to be a surprise attack and the BiH reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In general terms, was there a change in the capability and in respect to the ability of the ABiH 3rd Corps to counter HVO attacks?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Initially the HVO were very successful in their surprise offensive against the ABiH in the sort of Lasva Valley area from about the sort of 15th, 16th of April. And I could give you examples to illustrate why I believe that, should you wish. The situation was stabilised by the garrisons of Vitez and Kruscica, specifically, in holding out against superior force and then the ABiH were able to bring reinforcements from -- and specifically the 3rd Corps -- were able to bring reinforcements having disengaged their operations in the east and moved their soldiers and equipment west to mount a counterattack from roughly the Zenica direction, slightly around. And then essentially come in and reverse the tables on the HVO. And the ABiH by about the 21st of April had regained the initiative and were now in a very strong position in terms of their numbers in relation to the HVO in Central Bosnia. More specifically, they were militarily more capable. Numbers aren't necessarily the issue. They're what we would describe as their moral component, their morale, if you like. They were just more committed to the fighting, they were better at fighting, and they were better led. And they caused the HVO to be on the defensive. And it was at that point that we initiated a cease-fire and a process to disengage the two opposing factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Since you were mentioning the 21st of April, 1993, does the 21st of April, 1993 have a particular meaning for you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Well, it has particular meaning for me in that I found myself representing Colonel Stewart at a conference chaired by the ECMM ambassador and I was the senior UNPROFOR military representative, and the conference was designed to establish a cease-fire. It was supported at the highest levels, obviously, and the senior representatives of the HVO, Petkovic, and the ABiH HVO - I think I'm pronouncing it correctly - Halilovic, came down, supported by Blaskic supporting Petkovic; and Merdan, who was Hadzihasanovic's deputy, supporting 3rd Corps with Halilovic. Do you want to know more about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When you were -- or when you had the duty to broker a cease-fire agreement - I think that was the purpose of the different meetings you were referring to - what did you tell the representatives of the ABiH, including Merdan and Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I think it was a very difficult tactical situation for them to reconcile, in terms of the fact that they were now being successful in their prosecution of a counter-offensive against an enemy who had sort of taken advantage of them and taken advantage of their alliance. It was not difficult to convince the Croats to engage in a cease-fire for the first time. It had been impossible to convince them to engage in a cease-fire preceding that, when they thought they were winning. The challenge for Halilovic and Merdan was to recognise from our perspective that they were in a position to demonstrate strategic thinking, to understand that although they were militarily in a position to win this particular battle and they had militarily within their grasp Busovaca, which was a very emotional as well as physical command centre for the HVO and the whole -- the sort of Herceg-Bosna ideals, and they had to understand that despite this capability of winning this particular battle and taking revenge for the disloyalty, if you like, the behaviour - I'm grappling for the right word - the quite despicable behaviour of the HVO in terms of pursuing political advantages through military endeavour at an opportunity when the 3rd Corps in Central Bosnia were not able to reconcile this, they had to put that behind them and demonstrate a degree of what we described -- I described as generalship on the part of Halilovic in order for the greater good of his -- of the ABiH and the Muslim people generally to exercise restraint, exercise command and discipline over their forces, and from UNPROFOR's perspective -- my perspective representing UNPROFOR and UNPROFOR's perspective -- to retain the moral high ground in this situation in Central Bosnia, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Earlier on, Colonel, in describing the situation immediately prior to the 21st of April, 1993, you were making a comment that the ABiH 3rd Corps troops were led better. What made you conclude that in terms of leadership of troops the ABiH 3rd Corps was better at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: It's a subjective judgement on my part from my knowledge, personal knowledge and broader knowledge, of the two commanders, basically. And it has been my experience that the -- an organisation tends to reflect the quality of its commander. And Hadzihasanovic was a better military commander, in all senses that I would use to judge, than his opposite number in the HVO, Tihomir Blaskic. And I saw that personified, if you will, with the elements of the ABiH that I personally came in contact with. It wasn't a value judgement of their goals. It was simply a value judgement of the quality of their military officers that I met.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Earlier on at the beginning of your today's testimony you mentioned that money was collected in Brunei for the -- in broad terms -- for the Muslim cause in Bosnia. During the time you were deployed in Central Bosnia, did the ABiH possess, to your knowledge, the financial means to make things happen or to create circumstances that were in favour of the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: To my personal knowledge, no. We understood from other sources that weren't necessarily corroborated that the one thing that the ABiH wasn't short of was money. They were short of materiel. And paradoxically, despite their sort of local -- in our area of responsibility, their local superiority, if they could muster themselves in time and space, as they did for their counter-offensive in the Lasva Valley, they didn't have as strong a stream of potential reinforcements that the Serbs or the Bosnian Croats had. They had, if you like, no land link to an ethnically supportive nation. They, if you like, were sort of -- were ringed by potential enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I please suggest to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have our customary break. It is quarter to 4.00, and we will resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, did you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume with a few minutes delay, Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. There seems to be a slight technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, did you at the time you were deployed in Central Bosnia with BritBat, did you meet with then-Colonel Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. On a few occasions. And I have a recollection of speaking to him on the phone as well. I first met him in February at the -- in Kakanj at the Busovaca commission's inaugural meeting. I later met him at his headquarters in Zenica. I spoke to him on the phone -- at least, I think it was him. It was through an interpreter, so my belief was it was him. And the majority of my dealings, however, with the 3rd Corps were with Colonel Hadzihasanovic's deputy, Commander Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We will come to Merdan in a few minutes. Let's talk first about Hadzihasanovic. Having talked and met him a few times, what was your impression about his competence and his military abilities?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: My first impression of him when I first met him was of an intelligence man, a military officer who seemed capable of taking a operational or strategic perspective on issues, not getting overemotional about the tactical situation. I have a vivid recollection of him remonstrating with his HVO counterpart who didn't seem to be able to, on occasion, rise intellectually above the sort of tactical situation. He was respected by the other members of the commission and his peers as a capable military officer, which I later discovered to be the case. And so an intelligent, experienced and able military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just saying, Colonel, that he was respected. Does it mean that he was in command and control of his subordinate troops?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That would be my assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Being an intelligent, capable military commander, was the then-Colonel Hadzihasanovic aware on what was going on on the ground within 3rd Corps? Did he give you the impression that he was an informed commander?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, that was certainly my impression. And again, my total impression of Colonel Hadzihasanovic was not simply in my few meetings with him but was also in discussions with his subordinates, who were very clear of their confidence in their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You informed the Trial Chamber, sir, that you had more contact to Hadzihasanovic's deputy, namely Dzemal Merdan. How close was Hadzihasanovic to his deputy, Merdan?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Do you mean personally, which I really can't comment on, or geographically?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I mean, did Hadzihasanovic -- I mean in military terms. Did Hadzihasanovic get to know what Merdan got to know? Were they in each other's minds? In that respect.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That was certainly Merdan's perspective, that he was in the mind of his commander, Hadzihasanovic. And he reported and got guidance from Hadzihasanovic if he wasn't sure on the way to proceed within a particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform us on what occasions you did meet Merdan and what was the subject of discussions.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I met Merdan several times. He was detached to be the 3rd Corps representative with the Busovaca commission, which again was a demonstration from my perspective on Hadzihasanovic's commitment to that particular organisation as a means of establishing normality, or at least contributing to normality. So that further demonstrated my -- or impressed me with the commander of 3rd Corps's commitment to the situation. And where he was at the Busovaca commission, I met him several times, and we chatted. The most vivid occasion which we met was on the 21st of April, at the peace conference in the ECMM house in our base in Vitez, and we had both practical and philosophical discussions together with Halilovic, and I was again impressed with the quality of Merdan and also with -- by default with the quality of his organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: "Quality" means the professionalism? The military capabilities? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Quality of the individuals and also the quality of the organisation. I mean, I can't comment firsthand on the detail of how 3rd Corps ran its operations, other than on my visits to the corps headquarters there appeared to be a capable military infrastructure there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's briefly address one issue in respect to the capable military infrastructure within 3rd Corps. Did you get the impression that the ABiH 3rd Corps had the technical communication abilities to enable the commanders, including Hadzihasanovic and his deputy Merdan, to be informed?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: They could certainly communicate with each other. There was still a sort of land-line infrastructure within Central Bosnia, albeit we were excluded from it, as our telephones were switched off -- all but one, which nobody knew we had. The radio communication was slightly more problematic because of the terrain, and we relied on high frequency radios. They may have been able to put in place transmission boosters, because it was ground in which they had spent their entire sort of professional time, in that immediate context. I'm aware from discussions that there were difficulties in communicating to some subunits actually on the ground. We had incidents in order to implement the cease-fire after the 21st of April conference, where we had to support the HVO and the ABiH in transporting their commanders around the battle space to pass orders on to the ground. Whether that was a physical communication problem, i.e., that they didn't have radio communication, or whether that was the fact that radio communication couldn't convey the reality of those orders and they had to be given face to face, I was never quite sure. But they carried radio systems and they had access from different headquarters to telephone systems. And by and large whenever they wished to communicate with us, they could, and I took that as an indicator that they could communicate among themselves as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on, Colonel, to the last issue I wish to discuss with you today, namely the issue of Mujahedin. Did you get to know whether Mujahedin were operating within the ABiH 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: We understood that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge and from what you got to know whilst you were deployed in Central Bosnia within the ABiH 3rd Corps area of responsibility between February 1993 and May 1993, within which ABiH 3rd Corps military unit, if any, were the Mujahedin concentrated?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's quite a difficult question. I did not personally meet anybody who I could identify as Mujahedin. I occasionally was shot at by ABiH soldiers waving green flags and wearing green headbands which I presumed to be Mujahedin and would remonstrate with ABiH commanders as to objecting to being shot at. And in conversation with brigade-level commanders and other sources, my understanding was that "Mujahedin" was a term that was used to cover the more committed Muslim ABiH soldiers, whether they be foreign fighters who had come on a Jihad-type mission to Bosnia or they were Bosnian Muslim citizens who had a more fundamentalist view as to the future of their nation. We understood and I understood that the accommodation of these more -- stricter practicing Muslims had a sort of cultural clash with the more - how would I phrase that - the less -- the cultural norm for Islam within the majority of Bosnia that we knew and the majority of Muslims that we in the ABiH or citizens that we interfaced with were not strict Muslims that I had seen in other parts of the world, for example in the Middle East. And what I mean by that is their women -- they didn't subscribe to Sharia law, the women wouldn't go covered, they would drink beer. They had quite a Western interpretation of Islam. That probably isn't how they would interpret it; it's how I do. The stricter practicing Muslims, and specifically those coming from abroad, as sort of fighters, the mainstream of the ABiH found them quite difficult to accommodate because they were rather disillusioned by what they saw as a lack of adherence to Islam, and so they were concentrated in the 7th Brigade, which we understood was a brigade that consisted of soldiers who had a greater propensity to the detail of a slightly more Middle Eastern interpretation of the Koran and the practicing of Islam. I'm sorry I'm not being totally succinct, it's quite difficult because these were impressions. I never met the 7th Brigade, and understood, again, from discussion that they didn't particularly seek to meet UNPROFOR. And their reputation tended to precede them and their reputation for fighting and commitment to the cause was -- sort of kept them apart, in our understanding, from the majority of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How were the Mujahedin, who according to you were concentrated in the 7th Brigade - how were they used by the ABiH 3rd Corps in military terms?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: They were based on Zenica, as we understood. And unlike many of the brigades that we worked with within our AOR, which, if you like, were quite regionally-based brigades, the 7th was one of the manoeuvre brigades - there were others - and would be used to conduct offensives or to carry out operations which were specific to the intent of the corps commander at that time. If I give you views that I had received from the HVO, the HVO had a considerable fear of the 7th Brigade, disproportionate to any other brigade in many ways; and such terms as sort of "Mujahedin" created an effect if the minds of HVO soldiers opposing the BiH during the sort of April period totally disproportionate to the size of that brigade and its equipment. And so if you will, they had an ability to create an effect in the minds of their sort of opposition out of proportion to their actual size. And I viewed that as a considerable advantage to the command of the 3rd Corps in military terms, and I am sure -- and again, this is just a personal view -- that he was easily militarily astute enough to understand the effect the 7th Corps would have on the willingness to fight of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 3rd Corps commander in referring to "he"?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the issue of the Mujahedin ever been addressed with Hadzihasanovic and/or Merdan?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Specifically, no, other than personal curiosity on occasion to just try and get behind what this name "Mujahedin" actually meant in reality. And I've explained my understanding of that, which was foreign fighters plus Bosnians who were more comfortable in a more strictly Islamic infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what was the attitude of Hadzihasanovic and/or Merdan towards the Mujahedin issue?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I've never discussed that with Hadzihasanovic. I have recollections of discussing it with either Merdan or other commanders. And again, it was really professional curiosity more than anything else, built around, if you like, our own doctrine, which we describe as the manoeuvrist approach in conducting military operations, where we focus on the will of our enemy to fight us rather than focussing on their strength in materiel terms. So it's a case of an indirect approach, rather than an attritional approach. And I saw rightly or wrongly, from my own perspective, that the 3rd Corps with the concept of Mujahedin had a military capability to attack the will of their enemy, which would fit very well within our own understanding of the cleverest way to fight and would reflect on that from my personal perspective, on how I would use something like a force viewed as Mujahedin by my enemy and the conflict of interest that that may produce in my own mind. I can't put my own views into the mind of either Merdan or Hadzihasanovic, as it was my own personal reflections, but gained in discussions as to what this phenomenon of Mujahedin actually represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what were actually your own views?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: My own views were that they were a very capable asset, in terms of their ability to attack the will of an enemy to fight, and they would be used on what we would call our main effort. And I suspected as a professional officer that commander 3rd Corps would think in similar terms. And indeed we had reports of the Mujahedin or the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade deployed in many areas simultaneously, which patently meant they were not in all of them. And I would do a very similar thing, that sort disinformation, to strike terror into the hearts of my enemies as to the fact that my most capable brigade was facing all of them simultaneously. And again, I would suspect that commander 3rd Corps would be capable of very similar thoughts. I think the difficulty arose with the fact that certainly the foreign fighters were not necessarily aligned to the political and military intent that 3rd Corps represented as part of the ABiH. And I think I personally would have had a problem dealing with the capability that a concept like Mujahedin gave me with the effects of their extremist behaviour. And we had an example of that where two British mercenaries working with the ABiH were allegedly murdered by Mujahedin. They were certainly murdered; they had their throats cut. And we retrieved their bodies and buried them. And that sort of behaviour by an organisation, encapsulated with the idea of Mujahedin, would have presented considerable conflicts as to how one dealt with people whose very fanaticism, which was the cornerstone of their reputation, manifested itself in ways that were not consistent with the behaviour that I would expect from soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you get to know, Colonel, whether Hadzihasanovic, the 3rd Corps commander at the time, whether he undertook any efforts to solve the conflict? Or was he more, as you just described earlier on, in some sort of a dilemma - and you described it yourself - to be forced because of the military situation and because of the positive military effect of the Mujahedin to accept them?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: We certainly asked for an investigation into the murder of the two British mercenaries and understood that that had taken place. We never found out whether anybody had been held to account for it or not. And it wasn't that they were British or it wasn't that they were mercenaries; it was just that they were two dead members of the ABiH, or at least people who we understood to have attached themselves to the ABiH who had been murdered. And, of course, because they were British, we had a degree of interest in seeing people who had murdered them brought to account. We were never aware that happened. There were other incidents - and there were not many that came to our notice - of actions by the ABiH that resulted in what we would term as "murders", as opposed to sort of "military casualties." And when they were discovered, they were reported by us to the ABiH and we trusted the ABiH to pursue them with a full rigour. And we certainly had a view - that was the view as well of the commanding officer who knew Hadzihasanovic better than I did - that Hadzihasanovic had given his assurances on several occasions that incidents would be investigated, and we believed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I turn now to Defence counsel for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Watters. My name is Edina Residovic, and with my colleague Stephane Bourgon, I am representing General Hadzihasanovic. I wish to thank you for meeting with my colleague Stephane Bourgon prior to your testimony today. Colonel, you have already said that you have testified in this Tribunal three times, in the Blaskic, Kordic, and Kupreskic cases; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, you also made a statement for the Prosecution on the 6th and 7th of May, 2000 and on the 13th of May, 2000; is that correct too?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I certainly made statements. I will take your word that they were the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are not receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend the Prosecutor, you said that you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 6th of February, that you were deployed in Central Bosnia as a member of the British Battalion, and as deputy commander of the 1st Cheshire Battle Group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to being deputy commander, you were de facto Chief of Staff of the battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That is correct. I wouldn't call the 1st Cheshire a battle group. We would call it a battalion group. We were not equipped to fight battles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. But your battalion was well equipped for the mission that you had to perform within the United Nations forces; is it right to say that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: We were better equipped than most, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These were professional soldiers who before coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and before you yourself arrived, had special training to be able to carry out their mission in the wartime conditions that prevailed in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: As we were the first battalion group from the British Army to deploy to Bosnia as part of the United Nations, there was no precedent for what the conditions were that we would find. And so the pre-tour training planned by my predecessor, which I discussed with him at length, reflected a balance of procedures and drills that may or may not prove to be necessary in Bosnia. Future British battalions who deployed had training that more reflected the reality in Bosnia gained from the experience of ourselves and the battalion that replaced us, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. My learned friend also asked you about the communications that existed on the ground when you arrived. Is it right to say, Colonel, that in some situations you in your battalion did have to grapple with poor communications so that it would happen that Colonel Stewart, though he was the commander, frequently was unable to have full command over all units on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct. We were equipped with radios that did not suit the terrain of Bosnia in that our main command radio system was VHF, which is a line-of-sight system; also, it was old and unreliable. We also had to use high-frequency radio, HF radio, which is notoriously unreliable at certain times of the day, as it's affected by atmospherics. The result was when Colonel Stewart was deployed on the ground in his Warrior or in his Land Rover visiting a part of our organisation or the opposing factions, he would routinely be out of communications for extended periods of time and thus I would command in his absence as his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my second question as well. Want to with respect to communications that you knew the ABiH army had, would you agree with me if I say that those communications were functioning well towards superior commands - that is, from the corps to the higher levels of command - whereas communication to lower-level units were frequently interrupted and difficult to establish?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I would say that that would be a very fair supposition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said, answering a question from my learned friend, that upon arrival in Bosnia and Herzegovina you didn't know much about what was going on there and that once you arrived you did your best to learn a little more about the history of the Balkans and about Bosnia and Herzegovina; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I endeavoured to learn as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
