utterances.text: You studied the problem and you devoted your full attention to it, at least for the first 48 hours upon your arrival; but in view of the great problems you had to address, there was quite a bit of confusion in your mind and lack of clarity as to what was actually going on there.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you knew for certain was the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina had a year prior to that - that is, in April 1992, after the break-up of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - been recognised as an independent state and that after that she was admitted to United Nations membership. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That wasn't a factor that I focussed on. I think some of our interpreters, who were very proud of their country, told us these things. I don't have a memory of reading about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Colonel, but I think that your answer to my previous question has not been recorded, and my question was whether you had sought to find out more about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I know that you did so during the first 48 hours but that there was still some confusion left regarding the actual state of affairs over there. You did answer my question, but it wasn't recorded in the transcript, so could you answer it once again, please.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I think to say that the situation was confused is an understatement. I was endeavouring to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the legitimate armed force that was in the process of being formed at the time, the legitimate force and declared as such and defined by the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: My understanding was that within Bosnia there were three armies: Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Croat, and Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, throughout your stay there, you didn't try to find out which army was the legitimate armed force of Bosnia and Herzegovina but you accepted the situation on the ground as it was in fact.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That is the case. My understanding was that the legitimate army was an alliance between the HVO and the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of your arrival, did you know that as early as 1992 the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Republika Srpska had attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina and that already that year it had occupied more than 60 per cent of the territory of the state, in the north, north-east, and east of the country? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it was our reconnaissance as a group that established exactly the extent, from the UN's point of view, of the Serb aggression into -- Bosnian Serb aggression into Bosnia-Herzegovina, as on our deployment the United Nations did not have a definitive understanding of the extent to which the Serbs had pushed back the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a literal sense. And we spent a great deal of our time monitoring what we termed "the front lines" and spent a great deal of time visiting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the front lines towards the Serbian forces, or the forces of Republika Srpska, were the lines which marked the end of the area of responsibility of your battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Technically, no, because our area of responsibility extended in behind the Serb front lines. We did not have the combat power to force passage -- oppose passage through these lines, and so we were unable to exercise our responsibilities in those areas of our AOR that had been captured by the Serbs. Therefore, the de facto AOR, the pragmatic AOR, was that that was occupied by the HVO and the BiH forces, who did grant us passage into their different areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This demarcation line toward the Army of Republika Srpska was actually the front line or the defence line of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, more precisely of the 3rd Corps. And if you can confirm this for the Trial Chamber, it extended along a length between 250 and 300 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's an interesting question. It would depend on your perspective. We used the term "front lines" as the line whereby the ABiH and the HVO opposed the Serbs, and so it was either their defence line or the Serb's front line, and both terms are correct. It was the line that demarcated the advance of the Serbs and the point at which the 3rd Corps-ABiH-HVO had been able to hold the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was putting it to you that this line, if we look at it geographically from the west, north-west, was about 250 to 300 kilometres long and that three corps of the Serbian army were behind it: The Banja Luka, the Bosanski, and Romanijska Sarajevski [as interpreted] Corps. Would this statement be true, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: It is certainly true that there were Serb corps behind those lines. Ten years later, I'm sorry, I can't remember which they were. I know there was a Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived, you observed that both the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska and shortly after that some representatives of the international community as well started calling these armies on the basis of the ethnic composition of the majority members of those armies. They were referred to as the Serb, Croat, and Muslim armies. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's right within the colloquialisms of our organisation. We were quite clear that there was a differentiation between Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Croats, and Bosnian Muslims and Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in your communications with the Bosnian army and its commanders and political representatives, you knew full well that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a multi-ethnic army, regardless of the fact that some units were composed predominantly of Muslims, Bosniaks. Was that difference between the army and these other two armies?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I was only aware of one brigade that I would describe as a fully integrated brigade, a fully integrated multi-ethnic brigade. I was not aware personally of other parts of the ABiH and the HVO that I witnessed having a multi-ethnic chain of command. And so the manifestation to me was that they were the ABiH and the HVO, with the exception of this one brigade and they were an alliance that constituted the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is my perspective.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you can confirm many things that have to do with the structure of the army, its relation with the legitimate organs of power. And on the relations between the HVO and the BH army, with regard to all these matters, there are certain assumptions you have made. But you were never in a position to observe what their strategic objectives were or to observe what their legal basis was. You weren't in a position to obtain a clear perspective, a clear view of the armies in question.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: It was very clear to me in April that the strategic objectives of the HVO had nothing to do with what was in the best interests for the BiH or the Muslim people. And the Croat offensive of mid-April 1993 - and I should say the HVO, Bosnian Croat offensive - which at the time had the potential to involve Croatia, was conducted solely at the strategic level; certainly the operational level. You'd have to define "strategic" very carefully in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as you have already testified, you believed that the HVO and the BH army formed an alliance and together they attempted to oppose the Republika Srpska army. And this was the subject of the first meeting you attended in February 1993; is that your understanding of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you certainly knew from your commander and your predecessor that the HVO had previously attacked certain BH army positions in 1992, in Prozor, Novi Travnik, and Vakuf, and in January it did this in Busovaca and Kiseljak and in Gornji Vakuf. But with the assistant of members of the international community in Bosnia and Herzegovina a solution was found in order to establish a cease-fire. These conflicts were overcome. Is this the situation you were familiar with? Is this the knowledge you had when you assumed your duties?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes. But I think it would be naive to say that I believed, we believed, or the situation on the ground demonstrated that the conflicts were overcome as you stated. The situation in Gornji Vakuf continued, and there were constant exchanges of fire between the ABiH and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf throughout February and into March.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although at the time you didn't see any specific orders from the HVO on attacks, on ultimatums to the BH army, you saw that the HVO was attacking villages inhabited by Muslims; you saw that they erected checkpoints and prevented the BH army from passing through and they expelled the Muslim Bosniak population from the area of Busovaca and Kiseljak. Is that what you were able to see in the field, and is this what led you to the conclusion that you have just mentioned now?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The discussions in Geneva about the Vance-Owen Plan incited the HVO to use force to take over and surround territory that they thought belonged to them and they were following the example set by the Republika Srpska army. Would this be a correct description of the way in which the HVO behaved at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I would describe that they were incited, to use your word, by the Vance-Owen Plan to consolidate the populations within the designated cantons and to secure routes that they viewed as strategic, either within or between these cantons; and to do so they embarked on a programme of offensives which involved ethnic cleansing on a model that we had seen used by the Serbs, but equally one had seen it in other parts of the world as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the HVO sent an ultimatum to the BH army requesting that they disarm and place themselves under their command and then in April, as you have said, they organised a large-scale offensive in the Lasva Valley? They took over territory, expelled the Bosniak population, and Ahmici and other places were places in which serious crimes were committed by them.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't have a recollection of being aware of an HVO ultimatum being sent to the ABiH. But I agree with the rest of what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague from the Prosecution spoke to you about the military might of the HVO and the BH army. Would you agree with me if I said that after the attack of the JNA and the Republika Srpska army the BH army, which was still being established at the time, regardless of the number of troops they had, was in a fairly difficult situation and on the whole they attempted to hold the defence lines and to prevent the Serbian army from gaining access to other territory? For these reasons, it was in their interest to keep the HVO as an ally and they had no intention to fight a war with another enemy.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I think your comment "was in a fairly difficult situation" is an understatement. I think they were in an extremely critical situation. And would agree that it was a matter of their survival that the HVO was an ally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, if I may use the words used in a previous case, the army was like an island which was encircled. And now this is what I'm adding: In European countries, both near -- which were both near to it and which were further away from it, they couldn't find any allies that would support them. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That was my interpretation, that the Bosnian Muslims had no immediate ability to draw on allies to support them. They could only draw on the moral support of the wider Islamic world, and that support manifested itself both in a moral commitment to their cause and the pressure that that could bring within the world community and a number of individual or small group reinforcements of the type of people that have been described as Mujahedin and financial support. But critically, none of these two factors, financial support or the infiltration of small bands of Mujahedin, would enable, in my view, the ABiH to withstand an offensive by the Serbs and even with the support of the Bosnian Croats, the HVO, that support would be conditional on reinforcement from Croatia. In summary, you could describe them literally as having their backs to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the Republika Srpska army and the HVO had traditional allies in Europe, in certain European countries, then what is of special importance is the fact that they had the daily support of neighbouring states, the neighbouring state of Yugoslavia; and the HVO had the support of Croatia. This was not the case for the BH army.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: As I mentioned in my previous answer, that is correct. The ABiH did not have any neighbouring states who would lend support.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition, the HVO could count on continual support for logistics, arms, and other equipment that they needed to fight; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: And people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You pointed out that when performing your duties in one of the Islamic countries, in Brunei, you saw that money was being collected in order to assist the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, and subsequently, you never found out that that money was used for the BH army; and in particular you didn't have any information according to which the money collected in this way arrived in the territory of the 3rd Corps, was used for the needs of the 3rd Corps. Is what I have said correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Specifically for the 3rd Corps, no. We were aware from sources that money was able to make its way into the Muslim community within Central Bosnia. We were also aware that the ABiH was able to buy weapons and ammunition from other belligerents within Central Bosnia - bizarre as that may sound - specifically through Sarajevo. And in Tuzla we were also aware that logistics supplies, including arms and munitions, were delivered to the ABiH from air drop.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we spoke about military power, you mentioned a lot of factors that were important for an army to have power. Would it be correct to say that in the Blaskic case you said that without a doubt in spring 1993 the HVO was stronger than the BH army? It had supremacy. Would you stand by this claim today?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That was many years ago. I have no reason to change my view. I would probably in order -- for accuracy have to explain what I meant by -- if I had used the word "supremacy," what I meant by that. As I think I mentioned earlier today, and I can possibly best encapsulate this in the way we think about supremacy or what we describe as combat power, which we would articulate as having three components: A physical component, which is men and materiel; a moral component, which is a willingness to fight; and a conceptual or intellectual component, which is understanding how to fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When referring to manpower, to the human factor, would you agree with me if I said that if you take into consideration the number of brigades at the disposal of the HVO in Central Bosnia and the number of brigades that the Republika Srpska army had at the line of confrontation and the BH army had opposed them at all times, in such a case not even the number of troops of the BH army was greater than the number of troops that the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska had in combination.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm trying to understand. Are you asking me that the ABiH had a smaller number of available soldiers than the HVO and the Bosnian Serbs combined?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify the question. Very often the question is asked as to whether the number of troops in the BH army was once or twice the amount of the HVO troops. I'm now suggesting, because this is what you have testified about, that the BH army had to hold a 2 to 3 hundred kilometre line facing the Republika Srpska army. My question is: Given that the army had two enemies at all times, would it be correct to say that even in terms of manpower, if you take into consideration the manpower of the Republika Srpska army and the manpower of the HVO, if this is taken into consideration, the 3rd Corps didn't have supremacy in terms of simple physical power.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if my recollection is not wrong, I think the witness stated earlier on today in answering a question by my learned friend from the Defence that it was the ABiH and the HVO which were on the front lines towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, could you try to answer the question, because in a few seconds we will have to have our technical break. In line 8, page 56, a question was put to you. Try to answer this very complex question. And it would be good for you to read the question, think about the answer, and then answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the first thing to clarify is the term "brigades," because a brigade was not a specific organisation in the HVO or the ABiH. Different brigades were of very different size, and so it's not a currency with which to judge. The commitment of the ABiH to their front-line positions opposing the Serbs meant in Central Bosnia that they were not as capable as the HVO of assembling soldiers in time and space at the same tempo that the HVO were because more of 3rd Corps were deployed further east. And so if you take the totality, the BiH had in our view more actual soldiers. Whether those soldiers could be assembled to deal with, for example, an immediate threat was -- it would take time. So in Central Bosnia, the HVO could more quickly assemble a superior number of soldiers than could the BiH. But the number of soldiers isn't actually the critical aspect. That is merely one part of what I've described as combat power, which I did that rather laborious explanation. The means to fight is the physical component, and soldiers are part of the means to fight, as are other weapons systems that act as force multipliers within the physical component. And so I think it's a rather simplistic question to ask whether they had more or less. It would depend on what they could assemble in time and space to meet a particular threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's quarter to 6.00 now more or less. We will now adjourn and we will resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor again to Defence counsel. We normally adjourn at quarter to 7.00. If we don't want to keep the witness here until tomorrow, I would kindly ask Defence counsel to go to the essentials so that the cross-examination should be useful and so we can release the witness. Otherwise, he will be forced to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wish to address you. We looked at the time that we would need to complete our cross-examination, and further to your earlier ruling and to abide by that ruling, I shall certainly try and put the most important questions to the witness. But as I wish the witness to have sufficient time to hear the translation and for me to receive a translation of his answers, this slows down the process. So I would like to appeal to you, Your Honours, if we don't complete our cross-examination today, that we be allowed to continue it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try and finish it today. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, is it true that in canton number 10, which the HVO wanted completely to cleanse of the Bosniak population, that large towns such as Travnik, Bugojno, and Gornji Vakuf were majority Muslim towns and they were in this province? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I would have to see a map of the then-Vance-Owen proposed canton 10 to under oath say that those places were in it, as I can't remember the exact boundaries of canton 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But in any event, you do know that these were towns in which the majority population were Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was another matter that was of special strategic importance and that was the roads and communication links. And my question is: Is it right to say that the HVO wanted to gain control of the main road communications and to link up the so-called Croatian areas because it was common knowledge that who has control of the roads, he also controls the Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you said that the conflict started with Mate Boban's arrival in Travnik in April 1993, where the state colours of the Republic of Croatia were hoisted everywhere and when because those flags were torn down, the HVO attacked members of the army and killed two or three of those members. Is that approximately what you said in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'd say "the conflict started with Mate Boban's arrival in Travnik." But certainly, following his arrival and the appearance of the flags, there was a breaking down of the relationship between the Croat and Muslim populations, manifesting itself in a number of murders in Travnik. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that the HVO at the time took up positions around the town of Travnik and that it blocked all roads so that Travnik was virtually isolated in relation to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the HVO used the highly aggressive propaganda whereby it sought to frighten the Croat population and to force it to move to territories that were under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I was aware of a situation in Zenica where the ABiH - and we presumed it was the 7th Brigade - attempted to evict the minority Croat population, which we secured overnight in a church, contacted the 3rd Brigade headquarters -- 3rd Corps headquarters, sorry. And the mayor of Zenica intervened, secured the return of the Croat population to their homes in Zenica and personally guaranteed their security. I'm not aware that that population were required to leave Zenica by the HVO. And although there were rumours that minority HVO populations were being extorted to move, I personally didn't see it. I don't speak Serbo-Croat and so wouldn't have, myself, seen the means of this propaganda, leaflets or whatever. I don't know how this alleged propaganda took place. I had no personal knowledge of it, but I was aware of rumours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the HVO used their propaganda against UNPROFOR, claiming that UNPROFOR was transporting weapons for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That is correct. And claimed many other lies [Realtime transcript read in error: "lives"] as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the HVO resorted to intensive propaganda about the constant attacks of the BH army forces on all fronts, claiming that that army was committing massacres of Croats; and that in connection with such claims you did some investigations in several places -- Grahovcici, Guca Gora, Jelinak -- and that the findings of the British Battalion showed that there were no traces of any such crimes there? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to my previous question is transcribed as "and claimed other lives as well." I actually said "lies," not "lives". Madam, I'll just address your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the remark made by the witness, the transcript will make clear that the witness has clarified the meaning of his answer, that he didn't say "claimed other lives," But "lies." Is that, Colonel, what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please answer the question in line 23, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 23, the Defence is asking you a question regarding what happened at Grahovcici, Guca Gora, and you are being asked whether the British Battalion found any traces of war crimes there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, after the HVO atrocity in Ahmici, we received constant reports from the HVO of massacres of their people and we patrolled to investigate each of the allegations. I personally went to Grahovcici and Guca Gora; another patrol -- and found nothing -- We tasked another patrol, who went to Miletici, I think it was called -- yes, Miletici. And there they found five men had been murdered. And the accounts of the local people described it as having been committed by BiH soldiers who were not known to them and who had behaved in a way that hadn't been characteristic of other BiH soldiers that they had known. And we later recovered those five bodies. They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if I were to ask you now a question about the events in Miletici, would it be right to say that Miletici was visited by UNPROFOR and by the European observers and that the reports of both after talking to the population indicated that these murders can be -- had been committed by the Mujahedin? Would it be right to say that?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: This is very difficult. I don't remember seeing the word "Mujahedin" in the reports. They may well have been there. I haven't read those reports for ten years. They certainly, from my memory, were described as renegades or not the -- they didn't behave in the way that the ABiH soldiers had traditionally behaved towards the people in this village. They were not soldiers known to them. And they described them as something akin to renegades. I don't ever remember the word "Mujahedin." But as I've said earlier, I've found the term "Mujahedin" meant all things to all people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the other hand, the HVO not only in Ahmici but also in the villages of Nadioci, Santici, Hrusica [as interpreted], expelled the entire Bosniak population, killed a certain number of civilians, and totally destroyed these villages; is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition, the HVO used impermissible methods, that is, a bomb truck in old Vitez was used, so that you were forced to report that this was a war crime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct. We considered it essentially an act of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the fierceness of the HVO offensive and the crimes committed caught the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina by surprise and that they were shocked by the fact that their ally had betrayed them? Could that be put in that way?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: My meeting with the ABiH commander in Vitez on the morning of the -- I think it was 16th of April, I would -- my view of his reaction would concur with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, many of the UNPROFOR members like yourself felt that unless the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina halted further attacks, that this would virtually mean the end of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state. The army had their backs to the wall. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That is certainly the case in Central Bosnia. It obviously wouldn't be the case in, for example, Tuzla. But it certainly was the case in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, is it right that thanks primarily to one of the factors of combat readiness of the Bosnian army, that is, its readiness to defend lives, the army consolidated its ranks quickly and responded with a counter-offensive and managed to gain control of an important junction and restore control over part of the territory lost? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct. And from a professional point of view, I thought it was an outstanding piece of military conduct, military art.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the HVO asked for a cease-fire for the first time, though up until then it had refused to seize control over areas captured, it refused to cooperate, and it refused to allow the return of the population to the homes from which they had been evicted. This was the first time that the HVO was able to negotiate. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Not quite right. The HVO from the first morning of their offensive entered into negotiation for a cease-fire and essentially misrepresented their intention. In simple terms, they just told us lies upon lies. So they didn't fail to enter into a cease-fire negotiation; they did. But they -- it was quite plain to us after a while were essentially prevaricating with no intention of, A, telling us genuinely what they were doing, and with no intention of adhering to any of the cease-fire negotiations that they were having with us. That changed on the 21st of April, after the ABiH had re-established a superior position and were poised to attack Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend the Prosecutor, you referred to that meeting on the 21st of April and described the efforts of the army to halt the fighting with highly favourable terms and you felt that it was a significant contribution towards saving lives. Was that the attitude you took in relation to the efforts of the army commanders to establish a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: When you say "army commanders," do you mean the army commanders of the BiH and the HVO or just the BiH?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the army of Halilovic and Merdan, who participated in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: The procedure for this negotiation was after the initial meeting chaired by Ambassador Thebault, the ECMM ambassador, he then handed over the detail of a negotiation, having established a cease-fire in principle. The two delegations, the HVO and the BiH, were in two different rooms. I asked them to put the dispositions of their forces accurately onto maps for me individually so neither would -- the opposition would not see their dispositions and they would take my word that I would not divulge dispositions to either party. And essentially I saw it as my challenge to argue the case to the BiH for restraint. And I think my exact words, as they're burnt into my memory, were along the lines of, "The world community will judge you on the way you behaved today in the future. And I know as soldiers, I'm asking you to do a very difficult thing, and if you do it, you will save a great many lives, both of the people of Busovaca and Vitez and your own people in the future, as this war is bound to continue. Because the HVO are preparing to reinforce with regular forces from Prozor." I was very impressed with Halilovic and Merdan's disposition and the courage that they showed in being prepared to risk considerable criticism, I felt, personal criticism. And I was quite clear also that Merdan was operating with the authority of his corps commander, Hadzihasanovic. And so I was impressed with them and I think their action that day was statesmanlike and in the wider interest of all people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the commanders went directly to the lines and spoke to the subordinate commanders and they explained to the soldiers how important it was to reach this agreement and not to continue losing lives, both Bosniak and Croatian lives?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Not immediately, no. We had initially agreed a -- if my memory serves me, an immediate cessation of fighting and an initial withdrawal to a line we agreed on a map, withdrawing from Busovaca, I think it was north. I'd have to look at the map. But in the direction of Zenica, so away from the line of their advance, withdrawing over ground that they had already fought over. And they agreed to do that within 24 hours. About 12 hours after the conference, 3rd Corps got back to us to say that they were unable to achieve their withdrawal in 24 hours because they were having difficulty in contacting and convincing the soldiers on the ground that they should withdraw. We agreed that we would support both themselves and the HVO in the commanders personally going onto the ground to talk to the soldiers, their subunit commanders, and we achieved this by putting the commanders into our Warriors and taking them where they wished to go on the battlefield to visit their subordinate commanders and soldiers. And in doing that, they then convinced -- and sometimes with quite heated discussion and exercising considerable leadership -- they convinced their subordinate commanders of the requirement to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, at the time it was quite clear to you that the commanders of corps were issuing orders, but as far as the implementation of these orders were concerned, this depended to a large extent on the local commanders. And you are a witness of the fact that Merdan often engaged in negotiations and spoke to local commanders in order to ensure that the orders would be carried out. Is that the situation in the Armija in the spring in 1993? Is this the situation you were aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That was certainly the situation on the 22nd, 23rd, 24th of April, 1993 that I personally saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, it was a very reasonable decision of the commander of the 3rd Corps. He decided that by -- that he should go into the field himself and convince his commanders and troops of the importance of carrying out certain orders. He acted in this way in order to discipline his troops. Is that the conclusion that you would draw?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, it was clear to you that the 3rd Corps was being established and all the efforts made by the commander and his headquarters in fact made it possible to see that the BH army was getting better organised from day to day. It was becoming more professional than it was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I was aware that the commander of the 3rd Corps was taking a very personal, hands-on command, which is why he was unable to be represented at the conference on the 21st and was represented by his deputy, Merdan. As to what he was actually doing, I couldn't say, as I wasn't there. But the 3rd Corps responded having the local commanders being convinced of the rationale of the cease-fire and its architecture.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You praised the abilities of the command of the 3rd Corps and of his deputy and of part of the officers -- of some of the officers from the 3rd Corps headquarters. Would you agree with me if I said that the officers and the professional structure in the command, the structure of the commanders and the brigade commanders, is very important when ensuring the line of command and functions properly and when ensuring that there is discipline among the troops?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I would agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that when you were performing your duties in BritBat only 9 per cent of those in the 3rd Corps command had finished military training and half of the brigade commanders had no military education whatsoever, would you then agree with me that the corps commander had an extremely difficult task when trying to create the army and establish normal chains of command and ensuring that there was discipline among the troops?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, we were aware of the challenge that the 3rd Corps commander and his staff faced in what essentially was a citizen army, a militia, fighting for its survival.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that you drafted milinfosums in the BritBat and these milinfosums contained essential information that your company commanders and liaison officers and other personnel had obtained in the course of any given day. Would you agree with me if I said that the contents of such milinfosums frequently depended on the reliability of the sources from which you obtained certain information?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's why they were called information summaries. They didn't necessarily represent fact. They just represented the best interpretation of reality that we could establish on that day. So I would agree with you that they were totally reliant on the quality of the sources of the information as well as our interpretation of them, which also could be flawed on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that there was also the risk that certain rumours that were forwarded in your milinfosums could -- they could be dangerous because other parties, a third party, might take such information to be factual?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I don't know who the third party would be, because we didn't distribute milinfosums outside the United Nations chain of command, and I also don't quite know what you mean by "dangerous." Dangerous to whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, if you obtained information about the HVO according to which the BH army had committed certain acts and this hadn't been checked, if this was forwarded through your chain of command or through other international bodies and if this was then included in the daily -- in the weekly reports of, for example, the European monitors, in such cases such information might be taken to be fact in spite of the fact that its reliability had not been previously verified.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I would certainly agree that rumours could be transposed into people's belief that they represented fact. One of the challenges that we faced in trying to establish an understanding of reality in Bosnia at that time was the fact that Bosnia seemed to totally function on rumour. And one of our endeavours was to try and cross-reference as many of the rumours as we could, corroborated by our own people's observations and reports or not, as the case may be. And we were always quite clear what was a rumour, as opposed to what we understood might be a fact. I can't speak for how that could be misrepresented outside our own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about foreign combatants, the so-called Mujahedin, and you spoke about the 7th Muslim Brigade. My question is: Would it be correct to say that quite frequently certain rumours, criticisms, or stories about the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin came from the HVO in fact and the success of the 7th Muslim Brigade left quite a -- made quite an impression? The greater the successes of the Armija, the greater --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the question please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am turning to the Defence. The interpreters didn't quite seize the question. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, Colonel, that the various rumours about the 7th Muslim Brigade and about foreign combatants in that area came mostly from the HVO and in addition, as the BH army had more and more success, these rumours from the HVO were more widespread, became more widespread?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: Within -- yes, I would say that is a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll have 10 to 15 minutes for my questions tomorrow. I have tried to be as brief as possible. But I would like to request your permission to continue tomorrow if I can't conclude my cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you will need ten minutes. Does the other Defence team have the intention of asking this witness any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, we do have some questions to ask. We will need no more than 15 to 20 minutes at the most. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So ten minutes plus 15 minutes adds up to 25 minutes. I think that Mr. Withopf had additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, so far I can't see any questions. That may change after the Defence for the accused Kubura has asked their questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll continue for another ten minutes though. If you make an effort, I think we'll manage. If the questions are shorter, less convoluted, I think that the witness will be able to answer them easily. We'll try to conclude, because otherwise we will make the witness stay overnight for the sake of an additional 15 minutes of cross-examination. Mrs. Residovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you described the position of the BH army and you said that it was a very difficult one while you were performing your duties in Bosnia. If the corps commander felt the need to open up a third front, if he felt this was necessary, would you agree with me that he didn't have the forces to do such a thing and such a decision in those extremely difficult conditions couldn't be taken by him independently?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure who the third front would be against. And he would have been unwise to open a third front against the United Nations. I don't believe that the commander of the 3rd Corps had the necessary combat power to open a third front, as his two fronts were extremely difficult to simultaneously fight. And as we saw, if it hadn't have been for some quite outstanding military endeavour, they came very close to losing Central Bosnia. So the idea of a third front makes no sense to me at all. He wouldn't have been sensible to do it, and I can't believe for a moment that he could unilaterally have declared some third front.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to ask you to listen to an opinion of mine, and I would like you to comment on it. It concerns the issue of foreign combatants in the territory of the 3rd Corps. So as not to waste any time, I won't show you any documents, but I would like to present you with certain facts which you were perhaps aware of at the time and I would like to present you with other facts that you couldn't have been aware of at the time. Then I would like to ask you to comment on them. And this will be my last question for you. You said that you personally didn't have any contact with the foreign combatants, but you believed that they were linked to the 7th Muslim Brigade. You also said that they were linked to the BH army 3rd Corps. If I said that on the 13th of June, 1993 Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic reported to the Supreme Command Staff of the BH army about foreign combatants and local Bosniaks attached to them. And in that letter he said that these elements did not want to communicate with him. And he said that he knew that they were probably engaged in discussions at a higher level. In that same letter he asked for this issue to be resolved because he had no influence over them and he did not want to be held responsible for their acts in his territory. If you also were aware of the fact that two days later in response to this letter the commander of the BH army issued an order to Enver Hadzihasanovic requesting him to send them to Igman so that they could join the special unit linked to the Supreme Command Staff, and if I said that if they refused to do so he should refuse hospitality to them and he should disarm them. Furthermore, if you were aware of the fact on that on the same day when he received this order, Enver Hadzihasanovic, when speaking over the phone to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command said that carrying out this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this question. This question obviously overburdens the witness. Is question is meanwhile at the very least 20 lines long. I would ask, in compliance with what just has been said by the Trial Chamber, to break down the question in order to enable the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you break down the question, because it's a very long one. The Judges are following you, but the witness certainly finds it difficult to follow a question that is 50 lines long. So could you break up your question into its constituent factors and could you mention each factor individually.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can collect all these documents for the witness. If we'll be continuing tomorrow, he can then have a look at them and I will ask him very brief questions. I thought we would save time if I paraphrased evidence that has already been admitted. I can't do that if the I break the question down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. How many facts would you like to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five. Five facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead. Mention the five facts. Because the witness has told us that he is capable of following you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If in the course of a conversation on the phone General Hadzihasanovic informed the Chief of Staff that an attack against the Mujahedin would amount to opening up a third front and he asked for a new order telling him how to deal with the situation; and if towards the end of August the order signed by Commander Hadzihasanovic hadn't been carried out because they weren't under his command; if Commander Hadzihasanovic at the beginning of November in the course of a conversation with Cermud Gerantil [phoen], the chief of the ECMM in Zenica said that they were attempting to deal with the problem of the foreigners by placing them under their command or by sending them back to their countries; and if, finally, at the beginning of December General Williams informed the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, if you paralyse the Defence, we'll lose a lot of time. What do you want to say? Because the witness has told us that he's able to follow everything. And I think this was the last fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I certainly do not want to make things complicated. But my learned friend is asking the witness about his views on certain events or certain alleged events that went far beyond the time frame the witness spent in Bosnia. The witness was in Bosnia from February to May 1993, and we are hearing since three to four minutes nothing else than situations that were in November and December 1993 and maybe even later on. I find it very difficult that the Defence is allowed to ask such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the witness will integrate what you have just said in his answer. Some facts occurred after he left Bosnia and Herzegovina. The witness is a colonel and he knows how to deal with concepts. He can answer the question and can bear your comment in mind. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of December in a letter that the commander of the BritBat, General Williams, sent to the commander of UNPROFOR at the time, it was stated that the Mujahedin were not under the control of the commander of the 3rd Corps at the time - that was Commander Alagic - and in February the commander of the BH army met him in order to force them to recognise the command of the BH army. In such a case, Colonel, if we assume that all these facts are correct, would you agree with me that they indicate that the Mujahedin were elements outside the control of the 3rd Corps and Enver Hadzihasanovic, as commander, took the essential and reasonable measures required in order to solve this problem?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm aware from my conversations with BiH commanders - not with Hadzihasanovic but with Merdan and others - that the conduct of the Mujahedin, whoever they were and under whose -- under whatever command they were, presented a difficulty for the 3rd Corps. I don't believe up until I left in the middle of May that it would have made any military sense for Hadzihasanovic to deal with the difficulty that we were aware -- I was aware that the conduct of the Mujahedin presented, as he needed all the combat power he could get, despite the problems that -- and ill-discipline of the Mujahedin. However, I am reassured that you have said that once the position had stabilised, that Enver Hadzihasanovic was able to reconcile that situation and deal with the difficulties, both professional and legal, that the Mujahedin's conduct presented to the 3rd Corps particularly. And it would not surprise me, in my understanding of the commander of the 3rd Corps, that he would act in this way when the situation allowed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you would agree that what I have said is correct. They were not under the command and control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Residovic, the Chamber is getting impatient. How much more time do you need? Tell us. Otherwise, we'll have to delay things for tomorrow, because I think your questions touch upon questions that the other Defence team may have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm almost done, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you agree with me that Enver Hadzihasanovic did take all reasonable steps as commander in the way I have described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team, how many minutes do you need, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do need 15 minutes to go through a few questions that I have prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that we need another 15 minutes and that perhaps Mr. Withopf may have some re-examination, we will postpone the continuation of this hearing to tomorrow. Colonel, unfortunately the Chamber did its best to have you released this evening, but unfortunately the questions did not allow this. So we would like to ask you to come back tomorrow. The hear willing begin at 9.00. If the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic has a few more questions, I will give her the floor then. Then, therefore, could Madam Usher accompany the witness out of the courtroom, and we invite him to come back tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, just a few seconds. Could you tell us what you have planned for tomorrow. We have the continuation of this witness's testimony. Do we have another witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, yes, we have another witness ready for tomorrow, namely the one who is scheduled for tomorrow. And if you would allow me three to four minutes to address a number of issues that are related to the witness schedule. I can also do it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please continue, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can we for this purpose please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.13 p.m.,
